etymology: From biblical, of the Book; and sexuality, from Latin sexus, the division of male and female. The thing is older than the word, for God made them male and female in the beginning.
biblical_def: Biblical sexuality is the creational design God set in place before the fall and never repealed. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27); two sexes, fixed and good, not a spectrum nor a feeling. Upon this God built marriage: "Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh" (Gen 2:24) — one man and one woman, joined for life. Within that bond the marriage bed is honourable and undefiled; without it, the LORD calls His people to chastity, whether in the discipline of celibacy or in continence before marriage. Scripture names the alternatives sin: sodomy, fornication, adultery, and every desire that turns from God's order (Lev 18:22; Lev 20:13; Rom 1:18-32; 1 Cor 6:9-11; 1 Tim 1:9-10). Yet the same passage that lists such sinners adds, "and such were some of you: but ye are washed" (1 Cor 6:11) — mercy for the chief of sinners, not affirmation of the sin. The church loves the image-bearer caught in transgression, calls him to repentance, and points him to the washing. This dictionary confesses that God's good design is the only path of true blessing.
webster_summary: Sexuality, in Scripture, is the divinely fixed order of two sexes and one-flesh marriage between a man and a woman. All use of the body outside that bond is sin. The gospel offers cleansing, not the blessing of disobedience.
webster_full: BIBLICAL SEXUALITY, noun. The creational order of male and female and the one-flesh union of marriage, as revealed in Scripture and never repealed.
Founded upon Genesis: "male and female created he them" (Gen 1:27), and the leaving and cleaving of one man to one wife (Gen 2:24).
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge" (Heb 13:4).
It forbids fornication, adultery, sodomy, and all uncleanness; it requires chastity within marriage and continence without.
Its sanction is the wrath of God upon the disobedient, and its hope is the washing of the gospel for the repentant.
scriptures: Gen 1:27

Gen 2:24

And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
corruption_summary: The progressive and affirming movement rewrites the plain text, denying two fixed sexes and blessing what God names sin; this is corruption, not a fresh reading.
corruption_paragraphs: The affirming project, advanced by such writers as Matthew Vines and the late Rachel Held Evans, and by progressive teachers who would baptize same-sex unions, recasts the Levitical and Pauline prohibitions as bound to ancient context and so void today. Lev 18 and Lev 20 are said to address only cultic or exploitative acts; Rom 1:18-32 is read as condemning excess rather than the act; the terms in 1 Cor 6:9-11 and 1 Tim 1:9-10 are emptied of their plain meaning. The wider culture goes further, denying that the two sexes are real and fixed at all, replacing creation with self-definition and gender identity.

Against every such revision the church holds the text as it stands. Paul grounds the prohibition not in culture but in the Creator and creation itself (Rom 1:20-27); the apostolic vice-lists are no museum pieces but the standing verdict of God. To affirm what He condemns is not love but cruelty, leaving the sinner in his sin. True love for the image-bearer names the sin, preaches the cleansing blood, and walks with him out of bondage into the obedience of Christ — for such were some of you, but ye are washed.
roots_summary: The roots lie in creation itself, in the making of male and female and the institution of marriage in Eden.
roots_lines: Sexus (Latin) names the division of the race into male and female — a binary, not a spectrum.
Genesis 1-2 sets the pattern: two sexes made in God's image, joined in one flesh.
The Hebrew of Lev 18:22 and 20:13 names the act plainly as abomination before the LORD.
Paul in Romans 1 traces the disorder to the suppression of the truth about the Creator.
The gospel root is 1 Cor 6:11 — washed, sanctified, justified, for those who turn.
usage: The elder preached biblical sexuality as good news, calling sinners to the washing rather than leaving them in their chains.
Biblical sexuality denies the modern myth of a gender spectrum and confesses two fixed sexes.
She found in biblical sexuality not a cage but the freedom of God's good design.

etymology: From covenant, Latin convenire, to come together in agreement; and family, Latin familia, a household. A household gathered under God's covenant promise.
biblical_def: The covenant family is the household considered as a single unit standing under God's covenant promise. When the LORD spoke to Abraham He said, "And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee" (Gen 17:7). The promise is not to the believer alone but to the believer and his children, as the line of faith runs down the generations. So when the Philippian jailor asked what he must do to be saved, the answer was, "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house" (Acts 16:31). The household is addressed as one; the father's faith brings the whole family within the reach of the means of grace. This does not make every child elect by birth, for the children of promise are counted for the seed (Rom 9:8); yet it sets them in the place of privilege, under the word, the prayers, and the discipline of a believing home, marked by the sign of the covenant. The Reformed have always held that God deals with families and not bare individuals. This dictionary confesses the promise to believers and their seed, and calls every household to generational faithfulness.
webster_summary: A covenant family is a household set under God's covenant promise, the believer and his children together. The promise to Abraham and to the jailor's house teaches that God deals with families. The children are set in the place of privilege, not presumed regenerate.
webster_full: COVENANT FAMILY, noun. A household considered as a unit under the covenant promise of God to the believer and his seed.
Grounded in the Abrahamic word: "to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee" (Gen 17:7).
"Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house" (Acts 16:31).
It requires the believing parent to raise his children within the means of grace and the discipline of the home.
It promises that God ordinarily gathers His elect from the line of faith, generation after generation.

corruption_summary: The age treats the family as a loose contract of autonomous individuals; Scripture treats it as a covenant unit under God's promise.
corruption_paragraphs: The spirit of the age dissolves the household into a band of independent selves, bound only so long as each finds personal fulfilment, and reckons faith a private matter that no parent may press upon a child. The covenant child is reimagined as a blank autonomy who must one day choose for himself without the claim of God's promise resting upon him from the cradle.

Scripture knows nothing of such isolated individualism. God establishes His covenant with Abraham and his seed, baptizes households in the Acts, and commands fathers to bring up their children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The promise is to you and to your children. To raise a child outside the means of grace, presuming he will choose later, is to despise the very pattern by which God has been pleased to gather His people through the ages.
roots_summary: The roots are the Abrahamic covenant and its generational promise, carried forward into the household baptisms of the New Testament.
roots_lines: Convenire (Latin), to come together — God binding Himself to a people and their seed.
The Abrahamic promise of Gen 17:7 is the fountainhead of household religion.
Acts 16 records whole households — the jailor's, Lydia's — brought within the covenant.
Acts 2:39 carries the promise forward: unto you, and to your children.
The Reformed tradition reads the whole Bible as God dealing with families, not bare individuals.
usage: He understood his children as members of the covenant family, set under the promise from their earliest days.
A covenant family gathers for worship as one household, the father leading his seed before the LORD.
The doctrine of the covenant family answers the cold individualism of the age.

etymology: From household, those dwelling under one roof; religion, Latin religare, to bind fast. The binding of a whole house to God in daily worship.
biblical_def: Household religion, or family worship, is the daily worship of God within the home, led by the head of the house. The LORD charged Israel, "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up" (Deut 6:6-7). The home, not merely the sanctuary, is a school of faith. Joshua set the pattern for every father: "but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Josh 24:15) — the head of the house answering for the whole house. Abraham was commended because he would "command his children and his household after him" to keep the way of the LORD (Gen 18:19). The Puritans gathered their families morning and evening for the reading of Scripture, the singing of psalms, and prayer, and reckoned the father a priest in his own home, catechizing his children in the truths of the faith. This is no optional piety but the ordinary duty of the Christian head of household. This dictionary confesses that the family altar is the seedbed of the church, and calls every father to lead his house in serving the LORD.
webster_summary: Family worship is the daily worship of God in the home, led by its head, with Scripture, prayer, and praise. Deuteronomy commands the father to teach his children diligently. Joshua's vow — as for me and my house — is every father's charge.
webster_full: HOUSEHOLD RELIGION, noun. The daily worship and catechizing of a family in the home, conducted by its head.
Commanded in the Shema: teach the words of God diligently to thy children (Deut 6:6-7).
"but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Josh 24:15).
It requires the father to read the Scripture, lead in prayer, and instruct his children in the faith.
It promises a household trained in godliness and a church supplied from faithful homes.

corruption_summary: The age outsources a child's religion to school, screen, or peer, and empties the home of the family altar; Scripture lays the duty squarely on the father.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Rather it faces neglect. Many Christian homes have surrendered the daily altar, leaving the instruction of children to the Sunday hour, the screen, or the school, while the father sits silent at the head of a prayerless table. The duty is not denied so much as quietly abandoned.

The recovery is plain and old. Let the father gather his house morning and evening, open the Scripture, lead in prayer, sing the psalms, and catechize his children in the great truths of the faith, that the words of God may be in their hearts when they sit, walk, lie down, and rise up. Joshua's vow stands over every Christian home: as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
roots_summary: The roots are the Shema's charge to teach the children and Joshua's vow for his whole house.

etymology: From household, the family of a house; and faith, Latin fides, trust. The family of God, those of one faith dwelling as kin.
biblical_def: The household of faith is the family of God, the company of believers reckoned as kindred because they share one faith and one Father. Paul writes, "As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10). The church is no mere society of like-minded men but a household, for through adoption believers are made the sons of God and brethren to one another. "Now therefore ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Eph 2:19). The duty laid upon us is to do good unto all men — the love of neighbour reaches every man — yet with a special and prior claim upon those of the faith, even as a man cares first for his own house. "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith" (1 Tim 5:8). So the brethren bear one another's burdens, supply one another's wants, and love as a family loves. This dictionary confesses the church to be the household of God, and binds believers to do good to all, especially to the household of faith.
webster_summary: The household of faith is the family of God, believers made kin through adoption. Paul commands good unto all men, especially these. The love of the brethren has a special claim, as a man cares first for his own house.
webster_full: HOUSEHOLD OF FAITH, noun. The family of God, the body of believers reckoned as kindred in one faith.
Named by Paul: "them who are of the household of faith" (Gal 6:10).
"ye are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellowcitizens with the saints, and of the household of God" (Eph 2:19).
It requires doing good unto all men, with a special and prior care for fellow believers.
It promises the comfort of brethren who bear one another's burdens as a family.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the duty is often flattened. Some would erase any special love among believers as narrow or tribal, demanding an undifferentiated benevolence that loves all and so loves none in particular; others go the opposite way and care only for their own circle, forgetting the charge to do good unto all men.

Scripture orders love rather than abolishing its order. Believers are to do good unto all men, for every man is a neighbour; but they owe a special and prior love to the household of faith, as a man provides first for his own house. The church is a true family, knit by adoption into one Father's house, and its members bear one another's burdens and supply one another's wants.
roots_summary: The roots are the adoption of believers into God's family and Paul's charge to do good especially to the brethren.

etymology: From court, to seek favour as at a royal court; the season of seeking a wife with intent to marry, conducted in honour and purity.
biblical_def: Courtship is the godly, intentional pursuit of marriage, carried on in purity and under the oversight of family. It is not an end in itself but a season ordered toward the altar, in which a man seeks a wife to wed and not merely to enjoy. Scripture gives a pattern in the finding of a wife for Isaac, where Abraham sent his trusted servant, the family was consulted, and the LORD's leading was sought in prayer: "And the servant brought forth jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment, and gave them to Rebekah" (Gen 24:53), and the matter was laid before Bethuel and Laban. Such a path keeps the body pure, for "Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled" (Heb 13:4), and reserves the one-flesh union for the covenant. The young are charged, "Flee fornication" (1 Cor 6:18), and the older women to teach the younger to be discreet and chaste (Titus 2:5). Courtship therefore brings the wisdom of parents to bear, guards the heart from defrauding, and treats the other not as a means of recreation but as a brother or sister to be honoured. This dictionary confesses that the road to marriage must itself be holy, walked in purity and under godly counsel.
webster_summary: Courtship is the intentional, pure pursuit of marriage under family oversight. It seeks a spouse to wed, not to use, and reserves the one-flesh union for the covenant. Isaac's marriage gives the pattern of prayer, counsel, and honour.
webster_full: COURTSHIP, noun. The godly and intentional pursuit of marriage, in purity and under the oversight of family.
Patterned in the finding of a wife for Isaac, sought through a trusted servant and the family's consent (Gen 24).
"Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled" (Heb 13:4).
It requires purity of body, honour toward the other, and the counsel of parents.
It promises a marriage founded not on lust but on covenant and the leading of the LORD.

corruption_summary: The world has made the season before marriage a field of recreational dating and the hookup, severing intimacy from covenant; Scripture orders it toward the altar in purity.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning custom treats the season before marriage as a stretch of recreational dating with no settled aim, and the hookup culture goes further, prizing the pleasures of the marriage bed while refusing the covenant altogether. Intimacy is severed from intent, the body from the vow, and the young are taught to defraud one another and call it freedom.

Scripture orders this season toward marriage and guards it with purity. The pattern of Isaac and Rebekah shows prayer, the counsel of family, and honourable dealing; the apostolic charge is to flee fornication and to abstain, treating the younger women as sisters in all purity. Courtship is not a manufactured grievance against ordinary friendship between the sexes, but the simple recovery of a path to marriage that keeps the bed undefiled until the vow is made.
roots_summary: The roots are the patriarchal pattern of seeking a wife in prayer and family counsel, and the apostolic charge to purity.

Titus 2 charges the older women to teach the younger to be chaste.

Courtship guards the body and the heart while the road to the altar is walked.
Unlike the world's recreational dating, courtship keeps the bed undefiled until the vow.

etymology: From Latin natalis, of birth, from nasci, to be born. The conviction that the bearing of children is a blessing to be welcomed, not a burden to be avoided.
biblical_def: Natalism is the biblical conviction that children are a blessing and a heritage from the LORD, and that the bearing of them is good. The first word God spoke to man was a blessing of fruitfulness: "And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth" (Gen 1:28). The Psalmist sings the same, "Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. As arrows are in the hand of a mighty man; so are children of the youth. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of them" (Psa 127:3-5), and again, "thy children like olive plants round about thy table" (Psa 128:3). Throughout Scripture a full womb is a token of favour and barrenness a grief, for God opens and closes the womb according to His good pleasure. Children are not an accident to be managed away nor a drain upon the earth, but a reward, a quiverful, a heritage. This does not bind every conscience to a precise number, for the LORD gives to one many and to another few; but it forbids the spirit that despises fruitfulness. This dictionary confesses children to be a blessing of the LORD, and rebukes the barren spirit of the age.
webster_summary: Natalism is the conviction that children are a blessing and heritage of the LORD. God's first word to man was be fruitful and multiply. The Psalms call a quiverful of children a reward, not a burden.

Grounded in the creation mandate: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth" (Gen 1:28).
"Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward" (Psa 127:3).
It requires the welcoming of children as a reward and the rebuke of the spirit that despises them.
It promises the blessing of a full house and a quiver full of arrows.

corruption_summary: The progressive and anti-natalist spirit of the age treats children as a burden upon the planet and a threat to self, and population-control schemes would suppress the blessing God commanded.
corruption_paragraphs: A barren spirit grips the age. The anti-natalist movement reckons the bearing of children a selfish act, even a harm to the planet, and progressive population-control schemes have long pressed to suppress fertility in the name of crisis. Children are recast as a cost, a limit upon ambition, a strain upon resources — never the heritage and reward that the Scripture names them.

Against this the church confesses the first blessing God ever spoke: be fruitful and multiply. Children are an heritage of the LORD and the fruit of the womb His reward; happy is the man whose quiver is full. The church does not bind every conscience to a number, for the LORD apportions the womb as He wills; but it refuses the lie that fruitfulness is a curse, and it welcomes children as the gift God declared them to be.
roots_summary: The roots are the creation mandate to be fruitful and the Psalms' praise of children as a heritage of the LORD.

Throughout Scripture the LORD opens and closes the womb according to His pleasure.

etymology: From person, Latin persona; with the suffix -hood, the state or condition. The state of being a person, an image-bearer of God.
biblical_def: Personhood is the state of being a true human person, an image-bearer of God, borne not from some later threshold but from conception. The Psalmist confesses, "For thou hast possessed my reins: thou hast covered me in my mother's womb. I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made" (Psa 139:13-14), and that God saw his substance "yet being unperfect" (Psa 139:16). The LORD said to Jeremiah, "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee" (Jer 1:5). When Mary came to Elisabeth, the unborn John leaped in the womb for joy at the presence of the unborn Christ (Luke 1:41-44) — one unborn child rejoicing at another, both persons, both known of God. Personhood does not begin at birth, nor at viability, nor at the first breath, but at the moment God begins to knit the frame in secret. From this the sanctity of human life flows: man may not shed the innocent blood God Himself is forming. Abortion denies the unborn child his personhood, and so denies the testimony of Scripture. This dictionary confesses every human being a person and an image-bearer from conception, and stands against the shedding of innocent blood.
webster_summary: Personhood is the state of being a true human person and image-bearer, borne from conception. The Psalmist, Jeremiah, and the leaping unborn John all witness to life in the womb. Abortion denies the unborn his personhood and sheds innocent blood.
webster_full: PERSONHOOD, noun. The state of being a true human person and image-bearer of God, possessed from conception.
Witnessed by the Psalmist: "thou hast covered me in my mother's womb" (Psa 139:13).
"Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee" (Jer 1:5).
It requires the protection of the unborn as a person, and forbids the shedding of innocent blood.
It rests on the image of God, borne by every human being from the first.

corruption_summary: The age withholds personhood from the unborn to justify abortion, treating the image-bearer as mere tissue until some chosen threshold; Scripture grants personhood from conception.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning ideology denies personhood to the child in the womb, drawing arbitrary lines at viability, at birth, or at the appearance of some capacity, that the shedding of his blood may be called a right. The image-bearer is reduced to tissue, a clump of cells, a burden the mother may discard, and the testimony of Scripture is set aside as private religion.

Scripture grants no such line. God knits the frame in the womb, knows the child before he is formed, sanctifies him from the belly; the unborn John leaps for joy in the presence of the unborn Christ. Personhood is not earned at a threshold but borne from conception by the gift of God. To deny it is to deny the Maker who forms the child in secret, and to shed the innocent blood He hates.
roots_summary: The roots are the formation of the child in the womb in Psalm 139, Jeremiah, and the leaping of the unborn John in Luke 1.

etymology: From the Greek philoxenia, the love of strangers, from philos, love, and xenos, a stranger; through Latin hospitalitas, the kindness of a host.
biblical_def: Hospitality is philoxenia, the love of strangers — the opening of one's home and table to the saints and to the stranger for the sake of Christ and His gospel. Paul charges the church, "Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality" (Rom 12:13). The writer to the Hebrews adds a holy motive: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb 13:2), recalling Abraham at the oaks of Mamre. Peter urges it without grudging: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging" (1 Pet 4:9). So weighty is this grace that it stands among the qualifications of an elder, who must be "a lover of hospitality" (Titus 1:8; 1 Tim 3:2). The open home is no small thing: it shelters the travelling preacher, feeds the poor saint, gathers the lonely, and adorns the gospel before the watching world. It is the warm face of the household of faith turned outward. This dictionary confesses hospitality to be a Christian duty and an elder's mark, and calls every house to open its door without grudging.
webster_summary: Hospitality is philoxenia, the love of strangers, opening home and table to the saints and the stranger. Paul, Peter, and Hebrews command it; it is an elder's qualification. The open home serves the saints and adorns the gospel.
webster_full: HOSPITALITY, noun. The love of strangers; the opening of one's home and table to the saints and the stranger for Christ's sake.
Commanded by Paul: "given to hospitality" (Rom 12:13).
"Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares" (Heb 13:2).
It requires an open home without grudging, and stands among the qualifications of an elder.
It promises blessing to the host and the adorning of the gospel before the world.
scriptures: Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
1 Pet 4:9
Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
1 Tim 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
corruption_summary: The age trades the open home for paid entertainment and private comfort, and forgets the duty of the love of strangers; Scripture makes it a Christian grace and an elder's mark.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Rather it suffers neglect. The open home has given way to the closed door, the paid restaurant, and the guarded privacy of a busy and comfortable people; entertaining is reckoned a performance for the impressive rather than a love of strangers for Christ's sake. The lonely saint and the travelling brother find few tables set.

The recovery is the plain command: be given to hospitality, use it one to another without grudging, forget not to entertain strangers. The duty falls especially upon the elder, who must be a lover of hospitality. Let the Christian home stand open to the saints, the stranger, and the gospel's servants, that the love of the household of faith may be seen by all.
roots_summary: The roots are the Greek philoxenia, the love of strangers, embodied in Abraham at Mamre and commanded throughout the epistles.
roots_lines: Philoxenia (Greek), love of strangers — the heart of the duty.
Romans 12:13 commands the church to be given to hospitality.
Hebrews 13:2 recalls Abraham entertaining angels unawares at Mamre.
1 Peter 4:9 forbids grudging in the open home.
Titus 1:8 and 1 Tim 3:2 make it a qualification of the elder.
usage: Their hospitality kept an open table for the travelling preacher and the lonely widow alike.
Hospitality is philoxenia, the love of strangers, not the entertaining of the impressive.
An elder must be given to hospitality, his home a shelter for the saints.

etymology: From fear, dread or reverence; here the dread of man set above the dread of God. A snare that binds the soul to the opinions of men.
biblical_def: The fear of man is the besetting sin of dreading or pleasing men above God, so that a soul is governed by the faces of men rather than the face of the LORD. The proverb warns, "The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe" (Prov 29:25). It is a snare because it entangles the will, binding a man to the approval or the threats of his fellows until he forsakes his duty to God. Paul renounced it plainly: "For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). The rulers who believed on Christ yet would not confess Him show its grip, "for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God" (John 12:43). The cure is no mere boldness of temperament but the fear of the LORD, which casts out the fear of man as the greater dread swallows up the lesser. "Fear not them which kill the body" (Matt 10:28), said the Lord, "but rather fear him" who is able to destroy both soul and body. This dictionary confesses the fear of man a snare, and the fear of the LORD its only cure.
webster_summary: The fear of man is the snare of dreading or pleasing men above God. Proverbs calls it a snare; Paul renounces man-pleasing as inconsistent with serving Christ. The cure is the fear of the LORD, which swallows up the lesser dread.
webster_full: FEAR OF MAN, noun. The besetting sin of dreading or pleasing men above God, a snare to the soul.
Named in the proverb: "The fear of man bringeth a snare" (Prov 29:25).
"if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10).
It forbids the governing of conduct by the approval or threats of men.
Its cure is the fear of the LORD, in which the soul putteth its trust and is safe.
scriptures: Prov 29:25
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
John 12:43
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Matt 10:28
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: The age exalts the approval of the crowd and the dread of its disfavour into a ruling passion; Scripture names this a snare and points to the fear of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Yet the snare was never tighter. The age teaches a man to live by the approval of the crowd, to dread its disfavour above all, and to bend conscience and confession to the shifting opinions of men. The Christian feels the pull to soften the truth, to hide his Lord, to love the praise of men more than the praise of God.

Scripture names the bondage and gives the cure. The fear of man bringeth a snare, but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe. Paul would not be the servant of Christ and a pleaser of men at once. The remedy is not a bolder temper but a greater fear: let the dread of the living God, who can destroy both soul and body, swallow up the petty dread of men, and the soul is set free to obey.
roots_summary: The roots are the proverb that names the fear of man a snare and the gospel call to fear God rather than men.
roots_lines: Fear, dread — here, the dread of man usurping the place of God.
Proverbs 29:25 declares the fear of man a snare and trust in the LORD the safety.
Galatians 1:10 sets man-pleasing against the service of Christ.
John 12:43 exposes the rulers who loved the praise of men.
Matthew 10:28 commands the fear of God who can destroy soul and body.
usage: The fear of man held his tongue when he ought to have confessed Christ.
She broke the snare of the fear of man by setting the fear of the LORD before her eyes.
Paul renounced the fear of man as inconsistent with the service of Christ.

etymology: Mary, from the Hebrew Miriam; the virgin of Nazareth chosen of God to bear His Son according to the flesh.
biblical_def: Mary was the virgin of Nazareth whom God chose to bear His Son, truly honoured as the mother of our Lord, yet not to be venerated, prayed to, nor made a mediatrix of grace. The angel came to her, "And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God" (Luke 1:30), and she conceived by the Holy Ghost while yet a virgin (Luke 1:26-38). Elisabeth greeted her, "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb" (Luke 1:42), and Mary herself sang, "all generations shall call me blessed" (Luke 1:48) — words that exalt the grace of God toward a lowly handmaid, not her own merit. She was a sinner saved by the same grace as all, for she rejoiced in "God my Saviour" (Luke 1:47). We honour her as the most blessed of women and the true mother of the incarnate Lord; we do not pray to her, bow to her, nor lean upon her for mercy, for there is "one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). To turn the handmaid into a queen of heaven is to rob her Son of His glory. This dictionary confesses Mary honoured, but Christ alone adored.
webster_summary: Mary is the virgin of Nazareth, mother of the incarnate Lord, blessed among women. She is truly honoured but never venerated, prayed to, or made mediatrix. She herself rejoiced in God her Saviour, a sinner saved by grace.
webster_full: MARY, proper noun. The virgin of Nazareth chosen of God to bear His Son; honoured as the mother of the Lord, not venerated as a mediatrix.
Greeted by the angel: "thou hast found favour with God" (Luke 1:30).
"Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb" (Luke 1:42).
She is to be honoured as the mother of the incarnate Lord, but not prayed to nor adored.
She herself rejoiced in God her Saviour, confessing her need of the same grace as all.
scriptures: Luke 1:30
And the angel said unto her, Fear not, Mary: for thou hast found favour with God.
Luke 1:42
And she spake out with a loud voice, and said, Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb.
Luke 1:47
And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
1 Tim 2:5
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
corruption_summary: Rome has exalted the handmaid into a co-mediatrix and queen of heaven, binding to her dogmas Scripture never taught; the church honours her, but adores Christ alone.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome has heaped upon Mary a weight of dogma the Scripture never bore. She is declared immaculately conceived and so exempt from original sin; held to be a perpetual virgin who bore no other children, though the Gospels name His brethren; said to have been bodily assumed into heaven; and invoked as mediatrix, co-redemptrix, and queen of heaven, to whom the faithful pray and bow. So the lowly handmaid who rejoiced in God her Saviour is turned into an object of devotion that belongs to God alone.

Scripture honours Mary truly and adores her never. She is blessed among women, the favoured handmaid, the true mother of the incarnate Lord, and all generations rightly call her blessed. But she is a sinner saved by grace, who rejoiced in God her Saviour; she is not sinless, not a perpetual virgin, not assumed, not a mediatrix. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. To pray to Mary is to rob her Son of His sole glory; we honour the mother by adoring the Son alone.
roots_summary: The roots are the Annunciation and the Magnificat, where the favoured handmaid rejoices in God her Saviour.
roots_lines: Miriam (Hebrew), the name borne by the virgin of Nazareth.
Luke 1:26-38 records the Annunciation and the virgin conception by the Holy Ghost.
Luke 1:42 gives Elisabeth's greeting, "Blessed art thou among women."
Luke 1:47 has Mary rejoice in God her Saviour, confessing her own need of grace.
1 Timothy 2:5 sets the one Mediator against every Marian mediation.
usage: He honoured Mary as the blessed mother of the Lord, yet directed every prayer to Christ alone.
Mary herself rejoiced in God her Saviour, owning the same grace as every sinner.
The Reformed honour Mary but reject the Roman dogmas that make her a mediatrix.
